stories.topic: The 5,500 Crore Hole at Indian Bank (1995)
stories.summary: By the early 1990s, RBI had begun to dimly grasp that 'bank regulation' was a thing distinct from central planning. The 1995 discovery of a 5,500 crore NPA hole inside Indian Bank was the shock that finally pushed RBI to start thinking about prudential regulation in the modern sense. It was the first acknowledgement that the regulator's job was not to give orders to a 'family' of public banks, but to ensure those banks were actually solvent.
stories.insight: Bureaucracies typically reform only after a visible disaster. Until a number on a balance sheet forces the issue, central planners can convince themselves that the silence of the graveyard is the same thing as good performance.

stories.topic: The Rangarajan Committee Picked the Disk Controller
stories.summary: In the early 1990s, when computerisation came to Indian banks, the Rangarajan Committee did not just say 'banks should computerise' — it specified the CPU, the SMD disk controller, the operating system. Every bank in India simply implemented the RBI report as its IT strategy. The officials picking these chips were not embarrassed; they thought central planning of disk controllers was their job.
stories.insight: When government officials pick technical winners, you get the worst of both worlds — the same wrong choice frozen across an entire industry. The amusing concreteness of an SMD disk controller chosen for an entire country is the single best illustration of the central-planning mindset of Indian banking regulation.

stories.topic: Trucks of Share Certificates Choking the BSE (1993)
stories.summary: When foreign investment began trickling into India in 1993 — diddly numbers like $100 million a month — the Bombay Stock Exchange settlement system simply collapsed. The streets of Bombay filled with truckloads of physical share certificates being moved from one place to another. The BSE could not perform settlement; foreigners could not work this way. This concrete failure became the case for NSE, NSDL, and the Depositories Act.
stories.insight: The pre-reform Indian capital market wasn't 'inefficient' in some abstract sense — it was literal trucks of paper choking on tiny inflows. Every great institutional reform has a failure picture that finally makes change unstoppable.

stories.summary: Ajay recalls one of the happiest days of his life — the inauguration of NSDL at Nehru Centre. On stage were Bimal Jalan (RBI governor), DR Mehta (SEBI chairman), CB Bhave (MD of the depository), and P. Chidambaram (finance minister). Someone pressed a single carriage return to symbolise the first transaction; Chidambaram hugged Bhave; that was the ceremony. The Depositories Act, drafted by PJ Nayak and others, had to be passed by a minority government — and Manmohan Singh personally bubbled it up through the Congress political establishment to make it happen 'by hook or by crook.'
stories.insight: Big institutional change requires not just blueprints but a small group of people who will personally carry a draft law into a hostile political room and not let go. The hug at the inauguration is the iceberg tip of years of human effort below.

stories.topic: HDFC Had Never Repossessed a House
stories.summary: In the late 1990s, Deepak Parekh — head of HDFC, India's biggest home-loan company — told Ajay that in HDFC's entire history they had never repossessed a single house. Without SARFAESI, the lender had no real power to grab pledged collateral. This is what 'collateralised lending' looked like in India before the early 2000s.
stories.insight: The most basic feature of capitalism — that a lender can grab the asset when the borrower defaults — was simply absent in India until SARFAESI. You can't have a credit market without it; the trivial-sounding becomes load-bearing.

stories.topic: Mukesh Ambani's Driver and the Movie Theatre Tout
stories.summary: At an Indian Express event with Shekhar Gupta, KV Kamath, and Mukesh Ambani, Ambani described the financial-inclusion arc thus: in the bad old days, his drivers came to him for loans — there was no other way. Recently, walking into Metro cinema, a teenager plucked his sleeve to offer him a loan. That contrast — from driver-asks-boss to teenager-pitches-Ambani — is the credit-bureau-and-NBFC revolution in one image.
stories.insight: The expansion of household credit in India isn't a number on a chart — it's a shift in who can ask whom for a loan. When pitchmen are accosting billionaires in cinema lobbies, formal finance has finally reached the masses, even if imperfectly.

stories.summary: After releasing a ten-and-a-half-hour Seen and the Unseen 'Life and Times' episode with Ajay Shah, Amit got messages saying it was too short — listeners had wanted more on Indian finance specifically, which got squeezed out. This entire EIE episode 71 exists as the overflow chapter that did not fit in 10.5 hours.
stories.insight: Demand for serious long-form on Indian institutions vastly exceeds even very long content. There is a real audience for nuance — the constraint is supply, not demand.

stories.topic: The Locked-Room Mystery and the Melting Ice Cube
stories.summary: Amit detours into John Dickson Carr's The Hollow Man (1935), voted in 1981 the greatest locked-room mystery of all time. In it, Carr enumerates all the classic locked-room solutions — and one of them is a melting ice cube. Ajay had just used that exact metaphor for a firm in distress.
stories.insight: A pleasing accident of cross-domain language — bankruptcy theorists and detective novelists converged on the same image because the same physical fact (a thing that vanishes if you wait) actually drives both situations.

stories.summary: After the 2G spectrum auctions in Europe, every telco had massively overpaid; there was no real revenue in 2G, and one by one the firms went bankrupt. Yet for the consumer in France or Germany, nothing happened — phones kept working, numbers stayed, no dropped calls. Up in the financial superstructure, old shareholders and bondholders took the loss; new shareholders bought the firms as going concerns; the organisational capital was preserved.
stories.insight: The dream of bankruptcy is invisible bankruptcy. When an institution like the IBC works, the customer never notices that ownership has changed under the hood. Speed and predictability protect the firm's intangible capital — the people, the manuals, the tacit knowledge — that would otherwise melt away.

stories.topic: Maggie Thatcher Removed the Reporting Requirements on Purpose
stories.summary: When Britain freed up its current and capital accounts in the early 1980s, some advisors said: keep some reporting requirements, just for data. The reformers refused. Their reasoning: if you keep the queue and the form, some future government can shut the gate again with a single notification. The point of reform isn't to make the controls 'orderly' — the point is to destroy the architecture of control so that no future leftist can re-engage it.
stories.insight: Reforms must be designed against their future reversal. The capital-controls returning to India in 2015 (criminal clauses re-added to FEMA) prove the lesson: leaving the apparatus in place guarantees its eventual reactivation.

stories.topic: Oscar Wilde and the Fall of the Rupee
stories.summary: In Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), Miss Prism instructs Cecily: 'You will read your political economy in my absence. The chapter on the fall of the rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.' Indian monetary policy was so dramatic in the late nineteenth century that it had become a Wildean joke.
stories.insight: Indian monetary economics has a far older and more interesting history than the post-1947 story of fiscal dominance suggests. The bimetallic problems of the British Indian rupee were a global financial drama; we have collectively forgotten this.

stories.summary: Everybody in the bankruptcy field quotes Hemingway's line from The Sun Also Rises: 'How did you go bankrupt? Two ways. Gradually, and then suddenly.' Ajay calls it the single best description of how bankruptcy actually happens.
stories.insight: Hemingway nailed a deep nonlinearity. Distress accumulates invisibly until a tipping point, then collapses fast — a pattern equally true of banks, currencies, and political legitimacy.

stories.summary: At a meetup of EIE listeners in DC with Devika Kher and Pius (Aaditya Dar), a running joke emerged: every time Ajay says 'low-level equilibrium,' he actually means 'situation' (in the polite-Hindi-curse sense). Ajay accepted the code, with one defence: he uses it like 'a great South American novelist where everybody is good and pure and pursuing their self-interest, but the outcomes are just terrible — you're trapped in a horrible world.'
stories.insight: The agony of a low-level equilibrium is precisely that no one is the villain. Each individual rationally pursuing local incentives produces a collectively broken world. This is more depressing — and more accurate — than the Bollywood frame of evil capitalists or evil bureaucrats.

recommendations.item: The Journey of Indian Finance
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay Shah's chapter for the Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia, on which this entire episode is based.
recommendations.reason: A magisterial account of Indian finance from 1947 to the present, by a person who has not just studied but lived three decades of the journey. The definitive single piece on the subject.

recommendations.item: The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia
recommendations.creator: Edited by Latika Chaudhary, Tirthankar Roy, and Anand Swamy
recommendations.context: The compendium volume for which Ajay wrote the finance chapter; previous volumes had no chapter on finance.
recommendations.reason: Brings together the best people working on South Asian economic history, with a long-overdue dedicated chapter on finance. Ajay calls the table of contents 'drool' — a gorgeous book.

recommendations.item: Capital Ideas
recommendations.creator: Peter Bernstein
recommendations.context: Bernstein's intellectual history of modern finance.
recommendations.reason: Chronicles the emergence of the foundational ideas of modern finance — a great way to understand why finance is the brain of the economy and where the core concepts came from.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The EIE episode on how policy change happens — slowly, by communities, over decades.
recommendations.reason: Sets the template Ajay invokes throughout this episode — change is not certain, change is not permanent, and if you don't babysit a reform, it will go away.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's first-principles treatment of why finance exists and why it matters.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterclass in seeing finance not as 'rich people playing in an online casino' but as something that touches every aspect of ordinary life.

recommendations.item: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The recent EIE episode on India's 2015 shift to inflation targeting.
recommendations.reason: Background for the monetary-policy chapter of this episode; Amit promises 'movies will be made on this one day.'

recommendations.item: The Financial Expert
recommendations.creator: R. K. Narayan
recommendations.context: Narayan's novel about Margayya, an informal financial consultant in Malgudi — listed in the show's resources.
recommendations.reason: A literary entry point to Indian finance; one of the early Indian novels to dramatise a bank run and the precariousness of trust-based finance.

recommendations.item: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on classic economic fallacies hardwired into human cognition.
recommendations.reason: Background for Amit's claim that Marxism resonates because it speaks to instinctive zero-sum thinking; the fallacies episode unpacks why this happens.

recommendations.item: Larry White & the First Principles of Money (Episode 397, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Larry White
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with the economist Larry White on free banking.
recommendations.reason: Larry White showed historically that free banking — banks issuing their own currency — actually worked in many places without chaos. The intellectual ancestor of cryptocurrency arguments.

recommendations.item: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Episode 323, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Mohit Satyanand
recommendations.context: The episode recorded after Silicon Valley Bank's collapse.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's argument that bank failures are part of a healthy financial ecosystem — not catastrophes to be prevented at all costs. Also raises the new dynamic of weekend digital bank runs.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A long-form discussion of the 1991 liberalisation.
recommendations.reason: Companion listening for the partial-success story of the 1990s reforms in finance — what changed, what didn't.

recommendations.item: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (Episode 352, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Harsh Vardhan
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the banking expert Harsh Vardhan.
recommendations.reason: Where Harsh makes the opposite argument to Ajay — that India must build a great banking sector even if regulation is weak — the heartbreaking disagreement Ajay describes in this episode.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's economic-history-of-India episode.
recommendations.reason: Sets the broader context — including the post-1869 boom (Suez Canal, telegraph, Companies Act, Contract Act, BSE in 1874) that made India the first stock market in Asia.

recommendations.item: India's Pensions Disaster (Episode 65, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on how India's hard-won pension reform was allowed to wither.
recommendations.reason: Cited here as the canonical example of a reform that died from neglect rather than active reversal — a community dispersed, knowledge faded, and the gains slipped away.

recommendations.item: The 3 Globalizations (Episode 17, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the three waves of globalisation.
recommendations.reason: Background for Ajay's point that the first globalisation had no capital controls — passports, FERA-type laws, and currency restrictions are recent intrusions starting only with Nazi Germany.

recommendations.item: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah and Ajay Shah on capital-account convertibility
recommendations.creator: Bhargavi Zaveri and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their joint paper showing that Indian 'current account convertibility' is largely a delusion — the legal text actually bans almost everything by default.
recommendations.reason: The myth-busting reading for anyone who believed the 1993 announcement that India had achieved current-account convertibility. Reading the actual rules destroys the press-release version of the story.

recommendations.item: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeshwari Sengupta on de-facto convertibility
recommendations.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeshwari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Two-three papers including a recent Open Economies Review piece, demonstrating that India is more de-facto open on the capital account than China.
recommendations.reason: Empirical proof that the 'closed' Indian capital account is a fiction maintained by lawyers and accountants — the rich get out, the poor are choked, and the system functions as an employment guarantee for compliance professionals.

recommendations.item: The Constitution of Liberty
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's classic statement of the case for a free society — and the book Margaret Thatcher famously slammed down at her first cabinet meeting.
recommendations.reason: Amit's homage to Thatcher and his core intellectual lineage; bedrock reading on why capital controls and the rest of the unfreedom architecture are illegitimate at the level of first principles.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with the bureaucrat KP Krishnan.
recommendations.reason: Source of the story Ajay alludes to — Krishnan suggesting to Arun Jaitley that the FSLRC resolution-corporation draft be turned into a full bankruptcy code, which became the IBC.

recommendations.item: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (Episode 389, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah, who worked on the bankruptcy code.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation on the history of bankruptcy and the IBC's making with one of its drafters.

recommendations.item: The Hollow Man
recommendations.creator: John Dickson Carr
recommendations.context: A 1935 crime novel, voted in 1981 the greatest locked-room murder mystery of all time.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece in which Carr enumerates and demolishes all the classic locked-room solutions — including 'the melting ice cube,' the same metaphor Ajay uses for a firm sliding into bankruptcy.

recommendations.item: The Sun Also Rises
recommendations.creator: Ernest Hemingway
recommendations.context: Hemingway's 1926 novel of the Lost Generation.
recommendations.reason: Source of the most-quoted line in bankruptcy theory: 'How did you go bankrupt? Two ways. Gradually, and then suddenly.' A perfect description of how distress crystallises.

recommendations.item: The Good Lion
recommendations.creator: Ernest Hemingway
recommendations.context: Hemingway's children's story, in which a lion craves a 'Hindu trader sandwich.'
recommendations.reason: A lighter Hemingway corner with an exotic Indian-finance-relevant punchline — referenced as an in-joke about Hemingway's reach.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's foundational episode on public choice theory.
recommendations.reason: Background for Ajay's repeated claim that government failure is structural — a function of incentives, not personalities — and that 'there is no perfect government bureaucracy in the world.'

recommendations.item: What Really Happened?
recommendations.creator: Larry White
recommendations.context: Larry White's revisionist essay on the 2008 financial crisis.
recommendations.reason: Argues that the 2008 crisis was largely a failure of state overreach — distorted incentives created by US housing policy, monetary policy, and bailouts — not a failure of free markets.

recommendations.item: Not What They Had in Mind
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Arnold Kling's analysis of the 2008 crisis.
recommendations.reason: Companion to Larry White's essay — Kling marshals the case that government policies, not market freedoms, drove the crisis.

recommendations.item: Unchecked and Unbalanced
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Kling on the concentration of knowledge in private hands and the concentration of power in government — and the dysfunctional gap between them.
recommendations.reason: A systemic frame for Ajay's point: government will always be three moves behind the financial system because the smartest people work in finance, not in regulators.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's critical episode on India's 'digital public infrastructure.'
recommendations.reason: Background for the show's repeated worry that India's DPI/UPI is the same central-planning mindset as the Rangarajan Committee picking SMD disk controllers — a single state-mandated payment rail crowding out competition and future innovation.

recommendations.item: Premature Imitation and India's Flailing State
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Their paper on isomorphic mimicry in Indian public policy.
recommendations.reason: The academic statement of the concept Ajay invokes — Indian institutions that look like central banks or bond markets on the outside but lack the internal capabilities. Imported policies fail in India because local conditions differ.

recommendations.item: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (Episode 180, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: Amit's episode on isomorphic mimicry with the authors of the paper.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation behind the paper, on why Indian elites copy the form of Western institutions without the substance.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's 10.5-hour Life and Times episode on The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: The mother lode this entire episode is overflowing from. Listeners complained even 10.5 hours was too short, prompting Amit and Ajay to spin the Indian-finance chapter into its own episode.

core_ideas.concept: Finance Is the Brain of the Economy
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's foundational claim, repeated throughout: a modern financial system isn't a casino for the rich — it is the information-processing organ of the economy. It's about risk and time: bearing risky portfolios and moving cash flows across periods. 'Wall Street tells Main Street what to do.' Therefore having brilliant people in finance instead of particle physics is not a misallocation; finance shapes everything else.
core_ideas.quote: Finance is the brain of the economy. You want the best people to be in finance, because finance shapes everything else.

core_ideas.concept: The Four-Pillar Diagnosis of Indian Policy Failure
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's unified framework for what went wrong across all eight sectors of Indian finance: an intellectual failure of the Indian elite to build knowledge and community around four words — market failure, central planning, rule of law, state capability. We did central planning when we should have addressed market failure; we ignored rule of law; we naively gave regulators sweeping powers without public-choice skepticism. Every chapter of the story is a permutation of these four failures.
core_ideas.quote: It was an intellectual failure of the Indian elite to build the knowledge and community around words like market failure, central planning, rule of law, state capability.

core_ideas.concept: Capitalism Without Failure Is Socialism for the Rich
core_ideas.explanation: Bankruptcy is fundamental to capitalism — the Schumpeterian energy of the market economy depends on firms failing so the survivors can show a new way. If banks and other financial firms can never fail, you have not protected the system; you have privatised profit and socialised loss. The dignified version of failure is a predictable institutional script (the IBC's vision); the undignified version is power play in which the most thuggish creditor grabs the most assets.
core_ideas.quote: Capitalism without failure is socialism for the rich.

core_ideas.concept: The Melting Ice Cube — Why Speed Matters in Bankruptcy
core_ideas.explanation: A firm in distress is a melting ice cube. Once payments stop, vendors leave, machines go unmaintained, employees walk; tacit knowledge and organisational capital evaporate fast. The economic argument for speed in bankruptcy is not impatience — it is preservation. An ideal bankruptcy regime senses distress early, transfers ownership swiftly, and preserves the firm as a going concern (European 2G telecom did this; consumers never noticed). India's slow process means most firms are already destroyed by the time the law engages — only burial remains.
core_ideas.quote: A firm in distress is a melting ice cube.

core_ideas.concept: The Loss Has Already Happened — Bankruptcy Allocates, It Does Not Reverse
core_ideas.explanation: When a firm fails, the loss is over. The crying is done. All that remains is to allocate the loss across stakeholders (shareholders, bondholders, etc.). It is not a moment for recrimination, criminal investigation, or attempts to reverse the loss — that is the sunk-cost fallacy. The institutional task is purely about predictable allocation, ideally without raw power play.
core_ideas.quote: When a firm fails, the loss has already taken. All we are arguing about is who bears the loss.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's diagnostic concept (drawn from Rajagopalan and Tabarrok): India builds institutions that look like Western institutions on the outside — a building labelled 'central bank,' an exchange with screens, a bond market with depositories — but lack the internal capabilities. We have a bond market in name only; officials still set every interest rate. We had 'current account convertibility' announced in 1993, but reading the actual law shows it doesn't exist. Form without substance.
core_ideas.quote: Just because there is a building which carries a sign on it that says central bank or securities regulator, it doesn't make it the internal capabilities of one.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge and Community as the Engine of Reform
core_ideas.explanation: Real reform isn't a law passed by a government — it is a multi-decade ecosystem of researchers, bureaucrats, regulators, and academics who argue, write, debate, and slowly build shared understanding. The successful reforms (NSE, IBC, inflation targeting) had identifiable communities. When the community disperses, the reform reverses (pensions, equity-market governance post-2018). Hence the central task for the next 25 years is rebuilding knowledge and community, not drafting a single great law.
core_ideas.quote: We've thrown away that community, we've thrown away that team, and we're really back to a normal bumbling world of policy making.

core_ideas.concept: Babysit Your Reforms — Change Is Not Permanent
core_ideas.explanation: From the 'Long Road to Change' EIE episode: passing a reform is only the beginning. If you don't babysit it, the institutional gains erode. The criminal clauses of FERA were re-added to FEMA in 2015. Inflation targeting itself is now being sniped at by the left. Pension reform withered through neglect. Reforms aren't durable structures; they're delicate gardens that need constant tending.
core_ideas.quote: Change is not certain, change is not permanent. If you don't babysit a reform, it will go away.

core_ideas.concept: Capital Controls Always Hurt the Poor First
core_ideas.explanation: An apparent 'restriction on the rich' becomes an employment guarantee for lawyers, accountants, and civil servants — and a brick wall for everyone else. The de-facto convertibility of the Indian capital account is high (higher than China's, per Sengupta et al.), but only via expensive professional intermediaries. The rich get their money out; ordinary households are choked. The architecture of unfreedom is a regressive tax disguised as a populist measure.
core_ideas.quote: If you are able to afford the lawyers and the accountants, you are able to get a fair amount of openness on the capital account... You're getting an employment guarantee scheme for lawyers, accountants, civil servants, and you're choking off everybody in India who's not rich.

core_ideas.concept: Indian Regulators Pierce the Separation of Powers
core_ideas.explanation: Liberal democracies since the 17th century cut state power vertically — legislature makes laws, executive enforces them, judiciary punishes. Regulators worldwide already fuse two branches (writing and enforcing rules). India is uniquely terrible: regulators here also adjudicate, fusing all three. SEBI writes the rule, SEBI enforces the rule, SEBI rules on whether the rule was violated — and when you challenge, says 'I wrote the sentence, I understand it better than you.' This is violative of the basic structure of the constitution and awaits litigation.
core_ideas.quote: You're literally in a lawless land where the agencies control everything.

core_ideas.concept: Systemic Risk Is Not Just a Foreign Import
core_ideas.explanation: We started thinking about systemic risk through global crises (Asia 1997, LTCM 1998, GFC 2008). But Ajay's later view: India is entirely capable of generating systemic crises on its own, without any foreign trigger. Mishandled monetary policy + weak prudential regulation + no resolution mechanism = home-grown systemic crisis every few years. From 1992 to 2018, his paper documents six such crises — Andhra microfinance (2010), the COVID household-credit wave, and so on.
core_ideas.quote: The Indian financial system is entirely capable of generating a systemic crisis all on its own.

core_ideas.concept: The State Will Always Be Three Moves Behind
core_ideas.explanation: By the Lucas critique: once you set rules, very smart people optimise within them. Government cannot keep up because officials are weakly incentivised to figure out what is going on; the best minds are always working at the firms being regulated. This means crises will keep happening — they're a permanent feature of having a sophisticated financial system, like natural disasters. The mature attitude is grin-and-bear-it, not righteous outrage and reactive over-correction.
core_ideas.quote: The government will always be three moves behind.

core_ideas.concept: Financial Regulation as if State Capacity Mattered
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's project proposal title (echoing Schumacher's 'as if people mattered') — and his core late-career stance. Take the failures of the Indian state seriously. Don't optimistically assume better bureaucrats will fix things. In many cases, the right answer is to let go: do not have a banking system bigger than your regulatory and resolution capability can support. Take moral hazard seriously and change the architecture, rather than expanding ambition.
core_ideas.quote: Financial regulation as if state capacity mattered.

core_ideas.concept: If You Can't Run Air Traffic Control, Maybe Don't Have So Many Planes
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's heart-breaking metaphor for his disagreement with Harsh Vardhan on banking. Harsh says India must build a great banking system as the foundation of capitalism. Ajay says: if 25-35 years of trying haven't taught us banking regulation and bank resolution, then maybe the right strategy is to grow Indian finance through other rails — bond markets, NBFCs, debt venture funds, foreign banks regulated by foreign regulators. Use end-runs around the broken state capability rather than waiting another 25 years for it to learn.
core_ideas.quote: If we are a third world country and we don't know how to run air traffic control, then maybe you should not have so much air travel.

core_ideas.concept: Why Marx Always Wins the First Argument
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's aside: the ideas of the Communist Manifesto, however catastrophic in practice, will always resonate more easily than Hayek and Friedman. Why? Because Marxism speaks to our hardwired instincts — zero-sum thinking, top-down planning, the strongman of the tribe deciding everything. Liberty is software that has to be installed against the hardware. Hence eternal vigilance: every generation must re-fight for individual freedom because the default settings keep reasserting.
core_ideas.quote: Marx's ideas actually speak to our instinctive sense that things can be planned from the top down, that the world is zero sum, that you need a strong man of the tribe.

core_ideas.concept: Why Private Coordination Failed at the BSE
core_ideas.explanation: A puzzle Ajay says still troubles him. The 300-400 stockbrokers of the Bombay Stock Exchange could in principle have negotiated a Coasean bargain — modernise settlement, broaden membership, enforce against market manipulation — and built a great private exchange. They didn't. Why didn't private collaboration overcome the collective-action problem? Some bad actors were always inside the AOP, captured by manipulators, refusing to enforce on themselves. The state had to step in (SEBI, NSE, NSDL) — a less-good outcome than the failed private one would have been.
core_ideas.quote: Why were these people not able to come together and find a Coasean bargain?

core_ideas.concept: Bombay Is the Seat of Indian Finance — Don't Move the Regulators
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's plea against the geographical scattering of Indian financial institutions. The IRDA in Hyderabad (a Chandrababu Naidu deal), GIFT City in Ahmedabad — these don't work because finance is a tacit-knowledge industry. The endless human networks, person-to-person transmissions of knowledge, information, and culture happen only in Bombay. You wouldn't put the SEC anywhere outside New York; the same logic applies in India.
core_ideas.quote: The energy, the endless human networks, the quiet person-to-person transmissions of knowledge, information and culture — these happen in Bombay.

core_ideas.concept: The Counterfactual Cost of Public-Sector Banking
core_ideas.explanation: Roughly 5% of one year's Indian GDP has flowed from the taxpayer to the public sector banks since 1992 — a recurring transfer because the banks systematically underprice credit and don't recover enough cash flow to cover bad loans. Every economic downturn reveals another wave of NPAs. This is not a redistribution from rich to poor — it's a transfer from poor taxpayers to mismanagers of banks, and a destruction of wealth, not just a reshuffling.
core_ideas.quote: About five percent of one year's Indian GDP has gone as government money to the public sector banks.

core_ideas.concept: Indian Telecom as the Counterfactual Lesson for Banking
core_ideas.explanation: The pre-liberalisation telecom state: MTNL, BSNL, VSNL, DoT — government monopoly justified on national-security grounds, with one-payphone-per-village as the aspiration and seven-year waitlists for the rich. After Vajpayee-era reforms, with Sudhindra Kulkarni and Arun Shourie pushing private and foreign entry, India went to 1.1 billion phones for 1.4 billion people. The lesson: bureaucracies cannot deliver to the bottom 90% of an income pyramid; markets can. The Sam Pitroda hagiography misses this — what made the telecom revolution was markets, not technocrats.
core_ideas.quote: It is exactly as dead as telecom as a bureaucracy or steel as a bureaucracy.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on Ajay's career arc: 'Once upon a time you were the youngTurk of finance. Now you're just a middle-aged Indian sitting on a lawn... now you're just a YouTuber.' Ajay accepts the demotion.

Ajay's running joke about the Foreign Exchange Management Act vs. the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act: 'I don't know which word is more offensive.' Amit: 'I'd like a FIFA — Foreign Exchange Freedom Act.'
On the 10.5-hour Life and Times episode, listener feedback was that it was 'too short.' Amit: 'You didn't cover this, you should have covered that.' Hence this episode.

Amit on what would happen if podcasting were regulated like insurance: 'IPRA — Indian Podcasting Regulatory Association — what if it was in Karjat? What if a podcaster is taking positions on the shares that she is pushing? Have you considered that?' Ajay: 'They should certainly be regulated.'

On 'low-level equilibrium': Amit reveals that at a DC viewer meetup, the code was decided that whenever Ajay says 'low-level equilibrium' he actually means a polite-Hindi vulgarity ('it's a situation' — beep). Ajay's defence: 'I use it like a great South American novelist where everybody is good and pure and pursuing their self-interest, but the outcomes are just terrible.'

Ajay on Marxism's longevity: 'Some academic scribbler in the years gone by shapes the madmen in frenzy. And 1848 is a long time ago. But lo and behold, after independence, these ideas gathered momentum.' (Echoing Keynes's famous line.)
Ajay on his earlier credulity: 'I didn't understand implementation. Many years later, I started reading the damn laws.'

Amit warning Ajay on-air: 'You almost did today what you did in our Seen and the Unseen episode — you gave away my frickin' address. Luckily Gaurav cut it out. Today you didn't give the address, but you did say a tower in Varsova.' Ajay: 'On the screen for you right now is a precise tower where I one of your great achievements...'
Amit on Hemingway's children's tale: 'There's another Hemingway story which you must have read where there is a lion and the lion really badly wants to have a Hindu trader sandwich.'
Ajay on the false comfort of Indian bond markets: 'Things that are vaguely like a bond market are there. But actually... the officials will tell you what every interest rate is.'
Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises: 'How did you go bankrupt? Two ways. Gradually, and then suddenly.' The most-quoted line in the bankruptcy field.

Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), Miss Prism: 'Cecily, you will read your political economy in my absence. The chapter on the fall of the rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational.'
Merton Miller (banking): 'Banking is a 19th-century industry — banks just kept blowing up.' Quoted by Ajay to argue that bank failures are not the exception but the historical rule.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848): 'Centralisation of credit in the hands of the state by means of a national bank with state capital and an exclusive monopoly.' Ajay points out that post-independence India simply implemented this 100-year-old radical pamphlet.
Jawaharlal Nehru to JRD Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word.' The atmosphere in which post-1947 banking policy was set.
Margaret Thatcher slamming down Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty at her first cabinet meeting — Amit's homage to the British prime minister he calls 'a great hero of mine.'

Operation Sea Lion — the Nazi German plan for the invasion of Britain, invoked by Ajay to explain why the late-British-Empire period in India coincided with an imperial elite preoccupied with its own survival.
Williamson and North on institutions — the conception of bankruptcy not as a law but as a 'predictable script' that all parties pre-commit to, much of it evolvable voluntarily without state encoding.
John Dickson Carr's The Hollow Man (1935) — the locked-room novel in which 'the melting ice cube' is enumerated as a classic solution. Used to mirror Ajay's bankruptcy metaphor.

Indira Gandhi's slogan 'Garibi Hatao' — invoked sarcastically by Amit, who argues her bank nationalisations and economic policies kept hundreds of millions of Indians in poverty for decades longer than necessary.
